sections.history: Tiruvelvikudi lies north of the Kaveri in the Chola country, a short distance from Kuthalam in present-day Mayiladuthurai district. In the Tevaram it was sung by two of the three great saints, Sambandar and Sundarar, one hymn each, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam. The name joins velvi, the sacrificial rite, with kudi, a settlement: the place of the sacred rites. Tradition holds that the ceremonies before the divine wedding of Shiva and Parvati were performed here. The superstructure is regarded as early Chola in origin, and inscriptions of the age of Parantaka Chola, Sembiyan Mahadevi and Rajaraja Chola are reported from the temple, though the age of the first structure is not firmly known.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east and is entered through a three-tiered gopuram, with two enclosing prakaras around the sanctum in the Dravidian manner. In the sanctum Shiva is worshipped as a self-manifested linga, Kalyanasundareswarar, the beautiful bridegroom, while the goddess Parimala Sugantha Nayaki, the fragrant lady, is honoured in her own shrine. The sacred tank, the Kauthuka Bandhana Theertham, lies opposite the entrance gateway, so the pilgrim meets water before the deity. Because the marriage rites are held to have been completed in this tradition, the temple is said to have no separate shrine of the nine planets, a quiet mark of its character as a place of auspicious union.
sections.legends: The legend of Tiruvelvikudi belongs to the story of the divine wedding. When Parvati, said to have been born as the daughter of the sage Bharata at nearby Kuthalam, won Shiva as her bridegroom, the sacrificial rites that sanctify a marriage were performed here, with Brahma as the chief priest. The sacred thread was tied on the goddess in the ritual called Kauthuka Bandhana, and from this the place is also known as Kauthuka Bandhana Sthalam. Most accounts place the wedding itself at nearby Tirumanancheri, though a local tradition holds that it took place here. A second memory belongs to Sundarar, who is said to have bathed in the temple's Agni Theertham and been relieved of his affliction before singing his hymn to the Lord.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri in February or March and Panguni Uthiram in March or April are the principal festivals; Panguni Uthiram, the traditional day of the divine wedding, is kept here with special devotion. The monthly Pradosham is observed as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Tiruvelvikudi is a quiet village shrine, and it rewards a slow visit. Pause at the tank opposite the gateway, enter beneath the gopuram, and stand before Kalyanasundareswarar before turning to the goddess in her own shrine. The temple is regarded as a place of prayer for those whose marriage has been delayed, and families often come here on behalf of a son or daughter. Fields and village lanes surround the temple, and the stillness within its walls suits the thoughtful mood of the place.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tiruvelvikudi is about 3 km from Kuthalam, on the Mayiladuthurai–Kumbakonam road, and local buses and autos serve the route. Mayiladuthurai is the nearest major railway station, with Kumbakonam also within easy reach by road. Tiruchirappalli has the nearest major airport, a few hours away by road.
